heading: Far from home, faithful to God.
time: Daniel 1 opens the book. Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon besieges Jerusalem in the third year of King Jehoiakim (verse 1), about 605 BC. Young Daniel and his friends are taken to Babylon. The last verse jumps ahead about seventy years to the first year of King Cyrus, showing that Daniel stays faithful through the whole exile.

scenes.title: Jerusalem is taken
scenes.text: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem. The Bible says it was the Lord who gave King Jehoiakim into his hand. Some of the holy vessels from God’s temple are carried to the house of Babylon’s god.

scenes.title: Chosen for the king’s court
scenes.text: The best young men of Judah are chosen to be trained for three years in Babylon’s language and learning. They are given food from the king’s table and new names. Daniel becomes Belteshazzar; his friends become Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego.

scenes.title: Daniel makes up his mind
scenes.text: Daniel purposes in his heart not to defile himself with the king’s food and wine. He asks politely for a ten-day test: vegetables (“pulse”) and water. God gives Daniel favour with the official.

scenes.title: The ten-day test
scenes.text: After ten days, Daniel and his friends look healthier than all the others. They are allowed to keep their simple diet.

scenes.title: Ten times wiser
scenes.text: God gives the four young men knowledge and wisdom. Daniel also understands visions and dreams. The king finds them ten times better than all his wise men. Daniel continues until the first year of Cyrus.

symbols.title: The temple vessels
symbols.text: The holy vessels taken to Babylon return in chapter 5, when Belshazzar drinks from them at his feast. Ezra later records that Cyrus sent them back to Jerusalem.

symbols.title: New names
symbols.text: Babylon changes the young men’s names. Their Hebrew names honour the God of Israel; for example, Daniel means “God is my judge”. Babylon could change their names, but not their loyalty.

symbols.title: “Purposed in his heart”
symbols.text: Daniel’s choice starts inside, before anyone is watching. He then acts with respect and wisdom, asking for a fair test rather than starting a fight.

connections.title: A warning fulfilled
connections.text: About a century earlier, Isaiah warned King Hezekiah that treasures and descendants of the royal family would be carried to Babylon.

connections.title: Your body, God’s temple
connections.text: Paul teaches that our bodies belong to God and that whatever we eat or drink should be done to His glory.

connections.title: Wisdom comes from God
connections.text: Daniel and his friends did not become wise by their own skill alone. God gave it, as He promises to those who ask.

questions.question: Who gave Jehoiakim into Nebuchadnezzar’s hand?
questions.answer: The Lord did. Even in defeat, God was still in control.

questions.question: What did Daniel ask for during the ten-day test?
questions.answer: Pulse (vegetables) to eat and water to drink.

questions.question: Where did the young men’s wisdom come from?
questions.answer: God gave them knowledge, skill and wisdom.

interpretation.title: Why this story comes first
interpretation.text: Chapter 1 has no prophecy, but it sets the scene for the whole book. It shows God ruling over kings, and His people staying faithful in small, daily choices. Many readers, including this study, see Daniel’s diet as a lesson about honouring God with the body. The Bible itself does not say exactly why the king’s food would have defiled Daniel; it may have broken the food laws or been offered to idols.

reflection: What small, everyday choice could show that your loyalty belongs to God?
prayer: Lord, give me a heart like Daniel’s, faithful in small things and gentle with others. Amen.

heading: Bow to the image, or trust God in the fire.
time: Daniel 3 follows the statue dream of chapter 2. Nebuchadnezzar now builds a statue of gold, as if his kingdom would never pass away. Daniel himself does not appear in this chapter; the story is about his three friends.

scenes.title: A golden image on the plain
scenes.text: Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden image sixty cubits high on the plain of Dura. All the leaders are called together. When the music plays, everyone must bow and worship, or be thrown into a burning furnace. Everyone bows.

scenes.title: Three men stand
scenes.text: Some Chaldeans tell the king that three Jews he has put in charge, Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego, do not serve his gods or worship the golden image.

scenes.title: “But if not”
scenes.text: The furious king gives them one more chance. They answer calmly: our God is able to deliver us, and He will. But even if He does not, we will not serve your gods or worship your image.

scenes.title: Into the furnace
scenes.text: The furnace is heated seven times hotter. The strongest soldiers tie up the three men and throw them in. The flames kill the soldiers, and the three men fall down bound into the fire.

scenes.title: A fourth man in the fire
scenes.text: The king jumps up in shock. He sees four men walking free in the fire, unhurt, and the fourth looks “like the Son of God”. The three come out. Their hair is not singed, and they do not even smell of smoke.

scenes.title: The king praises God
scenes.text: Nebuchadnezzar blesses the God who sent His angel and saved His servants who trusted in Him. He makes a decree protecting their God, and promotes the three men.

symbols.title: An image all of gold
symbols.text: In chapter 2 only the head was gold, and it was followed by other kingdoms. A statue all of gold looks like Babylon refusing God’s message that its kingdom would end.

symbols.title: The fourth man
symbols.text: The king says the fourth looks like “the Son of God” and then says God “sent his angel”. Many Christians see here the presence of Christ Himself. Either way, God was with them in the fire.

symbols.title: Worship under pressure
symbols.text: God’s commandments forbid bowing to images. The three men obey God rather than the king, as the apostles later did.

connections.title: “When thou walkest through the fire”
connections.text: God promised Israel that the fire would not burn them, because He would be with them.

connections.title: An image and a death decree in Revelation
connections.text: Revelation 13 also describes an image that all must worship, with death for those who refuse. Daniel 3 shows that God can keep His people faithful in that kind of test.

connections.title: Faith that trusts without knowing the outcome
connections.text: Hebrews remembers those who “quenched the violence of fire” through faith, and others who suffered without being rescued in this life.

questions.question: What did the three men say if God chose not to deliver them?
questions.answer: They still would not serve the king’s gods or worship the golden image.

questions.question: How many men did the king see in the fire?
questions.answer: Four, walking loose and unhurt.

questions.question: What did the fire burn?
questions.answer: Only their ropes. Their bodies, hair and clothes were unharmed.

interpretation.title: Reading Daniel 3 alongside Revelation 13
interpretation.text: The Bible links the two passages through shared words: an image, worship, and death for refusing. Historicist readers see Daniel 3 as a picture of the final test over worship described in Revelation 13–14. That is a comparison of themes. Daniel 3 itself is a true story from Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, not a coded prophecy.

source: Biblical Research Institute: interpreting Daniel and Revelation
reflection: Can you trust God even when you don’t know how He will answer?
prayer: Lord, You walk with Your people through the fire. Give me courage to worship You alone. Amen.

heading: The most High rules in the kingdom of men.
time: Daniel 4 is a letter written by Nebuchadnezzar himself. He tells how God humbled him, probably late in his long reign. It is the last time we see him in the book; the next chapter jumps ahead to Belshazzar.

scenes.title: The king’s letter
scenes.text: Nebuchadnezzar writes to all nations to tell what the most high God has done for him. He begins with praise: God’s kingdom is everlasting.

scenes.title: A frightening dream
scenes.text: Resting in his palace, the king dreams a dream that frightens him. His wise men cannot explain it, so he calls Daniel.

scenes.title: The great tree
scenes.text: He sees a huge tree that reaches heaven and feeds everyone. A holy watcher from heaven orders it cut down, but the stump is to be left, bound with iron and brass, while “seven times” pass, so that people may know the most High rules.

scenes.title: “It is thou, O king”
scenes.text: Daniel is troubled, but tells the truth kindly. The tree is the king. He will be driven from people and live like an animal until he knows that God rules. Daniel urges him to turn from sin and show mercy to the poor.

scenes.title: Pride and fall
scenes.text: A year later the king boasts about the great Babylon he has built. At once a voice from heaven speaks, and he loses his reason and lives in the fields like an ox.

scenes.title: Restored and humble
scenes.text: At the end of the time, Nebuchadnezzar looks up to heaven, and his understanding returns. He praises the King of heaven, whose ways are right, and who is able to humble the proud.

symbols.title: The great tree
symbols.text: The tree is King Nebuchadnezzar, whose greatness reached to heaven and whose rule reached the ends of the earth (verses 20–22).

symbols.title: The stump left in the ground
symbols.text: His kingdom will be kept for him and given back, once he knows that the heavens rule (verse 26).

symbols.title: Seven times
symbols.text: The length of the king’s humbling. Many readers understand it as seven years. Verse 34 simply calls it “the end of the days”.

connections.title: Pride before a fall
connections.text: Proverbs warns that pride goes before destruction. Jesus taught that whoever exalts himself will be humbled.

connections.title: God sets up kings
connections.text: Daniel had already said this in chapter 2. Chapter 4 shows it happen to the most powerful king of his day.

questions.question: What lesson was the dream meant to teach?
questions.answer: That the most High rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever He wills.

questions.question: What did Daniel advise the king to do?
questions.answer: Break off his sins by righteousness and show mercy to the poor.

questions.question: When was the king’s understanding restored?
questions.answer: When he lifted his eyes to heaven and praised the most High.

interpretation.title: A real king, a lasting lesson
interpretation.text: The chapter tells what happened to Nebuchadnezzar and explains it plainly; it is not a time prophecy about later history. This study reads it as hope: God humbled the king in order to save him, and the story ends with the king praising God. We do not try to add details about his illness that the Bible does not give.

reflection: Where might pride be keeping you from seeing that God is in charge?
prayer: King of heaven, all Your works are truth. Keep me humble, and teach me to give You the glory. Amen.

heading: Weighed in the balances.
time: Daniel 5 jumps to the last night of Babylon, in 539 BC, more than twenty years after Nebuchadnezzar’s death. Daniel is now an old man. The visions of chapters 7 and 8 have already been given during Belshazzar’s reign. Babylon, the head of gold, now falls to the Medes and Persians, as chapter 2 said.

scenes.title: A feast with the temple vessels
scenes.text: King Belshazzar holds a great feast for a thousand lords. He calls for the gold and silver vessels from God’s temple, and they drink from them while praising idols.

scenes.title: A hand writes on the wall
scenes.text: Fingers of a man’s hand appear and write on the palace wall. The king is terrified, and his knees knock together. None of his wise men can read the writing.

scenes.title: The queen remembers Daniel
scenes.text: The queen reminds the king about Daniel, who had wisdom in Nebuchadnezzar’s day. Daniel is brought in and promised rich rewards.

scenes.title: Daniel’s rebuke
scenes.text: Daniel refuses the gifts. He reminds Belshazzar how God humbled Nebuchadnezzar. Belshazzar knew all this, yet he has not humbled his heart and has praised idols instead of the God who holds his breath.

scenes.title: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN
scenes.text: Daniel reads and explains the writing. God has numbered the kingdom and finished it. The king has been weighed and found wanting. The kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians.

scenes.title: That same night
scenes.text: Daniel is made third ruler in the kingdom. That night Belshazzar is killed, and Darius the Median takes the kingdom.

symbols.title: MENE
symbols.text: “God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it.” Babylon’s time is over.

symbols.title: TEKEL
symbols.text: “Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.” God has judged the king’s life.

symbols.title: PERES (UPHARSIN)
symbols.text: “Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.” The word sounds like the name “Persia”.

connections.title: The head of gold gives way to silver
connections.text: Daniel told Nebuchadnezzar that another, lesser kingdom would follow his. Chapter 8 names the ram as Media and Persia.

connections.title: Cyrus named in advance
connections.text: Isaiah named Cyrus as the one God would use to open the gates and set His people free.

connections.title: Babylon falls in Revelation
connections.text: Revelation uses Babylon’s fall to describe the end of a great end-time system that opposes God.

questions.question: Why was Belshazzar without excuse?
questions.answer: He knew what had happened to Nebuchadnezzar, yet he did not humble his heart.

questions.question: What does TEKEL mean?
questions.answer: You are weighed in the balances and found wanting.

questions.question: When was Belshazzar killed?
questions.answer: That same night.

interpretation.title: History confirms the setting
interpretation.text: For a long time Belshazzar was known only from the Bible. Babylonian records found later show that he ruled in Babylon as co-regent while his father Nabonidus was away. That explains why he could offer Daniel only the third place in the kingdom. Revelation’s “Babylon” is a separate end-time symbol; linking the two is a comparison, not something Daniel 5 says.

reflection: If your life were weighed today, what would you want God to find?
prayer: Lord, my breath is in Your hand. Help me to honour You and not waste the time You give. Amen.

heading: Daniel keeps praying, and God shuts the lions’ mouths.
time: Daniel 6 follows the fall of Babylon. Darius the Mede now rules, and Daniel, over eighty years old, is one of three top officials. This is the last story in the first half of the book. The following chapters return to Daniel’s visions.

scenes.title: No fault in Daniel
scenes.text: Darius sets 120 princes over the kingdom, with three presidents above them, and Daniel is first. Jealous officials look for a fault in Daniel but find none. They decide to use his faithfulness to his God against him.

scenes.title: A law that cannot be changed
scenes.text: The officials persuade Darius to sign a decree: for thirty days nobody may ask anything of any god or man except the king. Anyone who does will be thrown to the lions.

scenes.title: Windows open toward Jerusalem
scenes.text: Daniel knows the law is signed. He goes home and prays three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem, just as he always had. His enemies catch him and report it.

scenes.title: Into the den
scenes.text: The king tries all day to save Daniel, but the law cannot be changed. Daniel is thrown into the den. Darius says, “Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee.” A stone is sealed over the entrance.

scenes.title: “My God hath sent his angel”
scenes.text: The king cannot sleep. At dawn he runs to the den and calls out. Daniel answers that God sent His angel and shut the lions’ mouths. He is lifted out without a scratch, because he trusted in his God.

scenes.title: A decree for the living God
scenes.text: Daniel’s accusers are punished. Darius writes to all nations that everyone should fear the God of Daniel, the living God whose kingdom will never be destroyed. Daniel prospers under Darius and Cyrus.

symbols.title: Open windows toward Jerusalem
symbols.text: At the temple’s dedication, Solomon asked God to hear His people when they pray toward Jerusalem from a foreign land. Daniel prays the way he always had.

symbols.title: A law that cannot be changed
symbols.text: The law of the Medes and Persians could not be altered, even by the king. The trap depended on it.

symbols.title: The sealed stone
symbols.text: A stone is sealed over the den, and Daniel comes out alive in the morning. Many readers notice the echo of Jesus’ sealed tomb and His resurrection.

connections.title: Shut the mouths of lions
connections.text: Hebrews lists those who “through faith … stopped the mouths of lions”.

connections.title: Faithful in prayer
connections.text: Paul urges believers to pray without ceasing. Jesus taught us to pray to our Father in secret.

connections.title: A test of loyalty at the end
connections.text: Revelation describes a law that forces worship. Like Daniel 3, this story shows God’s people staying loyal under such pressure.

questions.question: Why could Daniel’s enemies find no fault in him?
questions.answer: He was faithful, and no error or fault was found in him.

questions.question: What did Daniel do after the decree was signed?
questions.answer: He prayed three times a day, as he did before.

questions.question: Why was no hurt found on Daniel?
questions.answer: Because he believed in his God.

interpretation.title: Who was Darius the Mede?
interpretation.text: The Bible says Darius the Mede took the kingdom at about 62 years old and later mentions Cyrus the Persian. Outside the Bible, historians have not found a record under this name, and they suggest different identifications. This study does not pick one. The point of the story is clear: God protects those who are faithful to Him.

reflection: What habit of prayer would you want to keep even if it cost you something?
prayer: Living God, You deliver and rescue. Help me to serve You continually, as Daniel did. Amen.

heading: Beasts rise, but the Son of man receives the kingdom.
time: Daniel 7 goes back in time. Daniel has this dream in the first year of King Belshazzar (verse 1), before Babylon falls in chapter 5. It is the first vision Daniel himself receives. It covers the same history as the king’s statue dream in chapter 2, then adds a judgment in heaven and more detail about the last power on earth.

scenes.title: Four beasts from a stormy sea
scenes.text: Daniel writes down a dream he had at night. The four winds stir up the great sea, and four great beasts come up out of it. Each one is different.

scenes.title: A lion, a bear, a leopard and a terrible beast
scenes.text: The first beast is like a lion with eagle’s wings. The second is like a bear with three ribs in its mouth. The third is like a leopard with four wings and four heads. The fourth is terrible, with great iron teeth and ten horns. Then a little horn grows up among them, pulls out three horns, and has eyes like a man and a mouth speaking great things.

scenes.title: The court in heaven
scenes.text: Thrones are set, and the Ancient of days sits down. Thousands upon thousands serve Him. The judgment begins and the books are opened. Because of the horn’s proud words, the beast is destroyed.

scenes.title: One like the Son of man
scenes.text: One like the Son of man comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of days. He is given an everlasting kingdom that will never pass away or be destroyed.

scenes.title: The short explanation
scenes.text: The vision troubles Daniel, so he asks one of those standing nearby what it means. He is told that the four beasts are four kings, and that the saints of the most High will receive the kingdom for ever.

scenes.title: Daniel asks about the fourth beast
scenes.text: Daniel wants to know more about the fourth beast, its ten horns and the little horn. He sees the horn make war with the saints until the Ancient of days comes and judgment is given to the saints.

scenes.title: The longer explanation
scenes.text: The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom, and the ten horns are ten kings. Another king rises after them and puts down three. He speaks against the most High, wears out the saints and thinks to change times and laws, for “a time and times and the dividing of time”. Then the judgment sits, his power is taken away, and the kingdom is given to the saints.

scenes.title: Daniel keeps it in his heart
scenes.text: The vision leaves Daniel troubled and pale, but he keeps the matter in his heart.

symbols.title: Four great beasts
symbols.text: Four kings, or kingdoms. Verse 17 calls the beasts four kings, and verse 23 calls the fourth beast the fourth kingdom. A wild beast is a picture of a ruling power.

symbols.title: Ten horns
symbols.text: Ten kings that arise out of the fourth kingdom (verse 24). In the Bible a horn often pictures strength or power. A further king, the little horn, rises after them.

symbols.title: A time and times and the dividing of time
symbols.text: Revelation uses the same phrase and also gives the same period as 1,260 days and as 42 months. So “a time” is one year, “times” is two years and “the dividing of time” is half a year: three and a half prophetic years.

connections.title: The same story as the statue
connections.text: In chapter 2 a statue of gold, silver, brass and iron is struck by a stone that becomes an everlasting kingdom. In chapter 7 four beasts are followed by the kingdom given to the Son of man and the saints. Both visions cover four kingdoms and end with God’s kingdom.

connections.title: The Son of man
connections.text: Jesus often called Himself the Son of man. At His trial He used Daniel’s words, saying they would see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven. Revelation 1 describes Him as one like the Son of man.

connections.title: Echoes in Revelation 13
connections.text: Revelation’s beast from the sea has parts of a leopard, a bear and a lion, ten horns, a mouth speaking great things, and power for 42 months. John is drawing on the pictures of Daniel 7.

questions.question: What are the four beasts?
questions.answer: Four kings, or kingdoms, that arise on the earth.

questions.question: Who receives the kingdom that never ends?
questions.answer: One like the Son of man receives it, and the saints of the most High share in it.

questions.question: What happens in heaven before the little horn loses its power?
questions.answer: The judgment sits and the books are opened. Then his dominion is taken away.

calculation.title: How long is “a time and times and the dividing of time”?
calculation.intro: The first three steps come from the Bible. The last two apply them to history, and that is interpretation. The dates follow Amazing Facts.

steps.title: Three and a half “times”
steps.text: The little horn has power over the saints for a time, times and the dividing of time. Revelation uses the same words for the woman in the wilderness.

steps.title: 1,260 days, or 42 months
steps.text: Revelation also describes this period as 1,260 days and as 42 months. 42 months of 30 days are 1,260 days.

steps.title: A day for a year
steps.text: In some prophecies God uses one day to stand for one year. Symbolic prophecies are often read this way, because the beasts and horns are symbols too.

steps.title: Three horns plucked up: 493, 534 and 538
steps.text: Amazing Facts identifies the three horns plucked up before the little horn as three Arian kingdoms that opposed the bishop of Rome: the Heruli (eradicated in 493), the Vandals (534) and the Ostrogoths (538).

steps.title: 1,260 years: AD 538 to 1798
steps.text: Following Amazing Facts, this study takes the period as 1,260 years. It begins in AD 538, when the last of the three opposing Arian kingdoms, the Ostrogoths, was uprooted. It ends in 1798, when Napoleon’s general Berthier took the pope captive, the “deadly wound” of Revelation 13:3.

interpretation.title: How this study reads the beasts and the little horn
interpretation.text: Daniel 7 says the beasts are kingdoms but does not name them. Comparing chapters 2 and 8, historicist readers identify them as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome. The ten horns are read as the kingdoms that came out of divided Rome, and the little horn as the papacy as a religious and political power in the Middle Ages. These identifications are interpretation, not words written in Daniel 7. They describe a system and its claims, not the faith of individual Catholics. Other Christians read the chapter differently.

source: Biblical Research Institute: interpreting Daniel and Revelation
Amazing Facts: Who Is the Antichrist?
reflection: When the world seems ruled by fierce powers, what difference does it make that the last kingdom belongs to the Son of man?
prayer: Lord Jesus, Your kingdom will never pass away. Help me to stay faithful to You and to trust Your judgment. Amen.

heading: Powers push and fall. The sanctuary will be cleansed.
time: Two years after chapter 7, in the third year of Belshazzar (verse 1), Daniel receives a second vision. Babylon is about to fall, so this vision starts with Medo-Persia. Gabriel says it reaches to “the time of the end” (verse 17). Its pictures match the bear and leopard of chapter 7, but this time the kingdoms are named.

scenes.title: A vision at Shushan
scenes.text: In the vision Daniel finds himself at Shushan, in the province of Elam, beside the river Ulai.

scenes.title: A ram with two horns
scenes.text: A ram with two high horns stands by the river. One horn is higher, and it came up last. The ram pushes west, north and south, and no beast can stand against him.

scenes.title: A goat from the west
scenes.text: A goat with one great horn between his eyes rushes from the west without touching the ground. He breaks the ram’s two horns. When the goat is strongest, the great horn is broken, and four horns grow up toward the four winds of heaven.

scenes.title: A little horn grows very great
scenes.text: A little horn grows toward the south, the east and the pleasant land. It reaches up to the host of heaven and magnifies itself against the Prince of the host. The daily is taken away, the place of His sanctuary is cast down, and truth is thrown to the ground.

scenes.title: How long?
scenes.text: One holy one asks another how long the vision will last. The answer comes: “Unto two thousand and three hundred days; then shall the sanctuary be cleansed.”

scenes.title: Gabriel is sent
scenes.text: A voice tells Gabriel to make Daniel understand the vision. Daniel falls on his face, afraid. Gabriel touches him, sets him upright and says the vision is for the time of the end.

scenes.title: The ram and the goat explained
scenes.text: The ram is the kings of Media and Persia. The goat is the king of Grecia, and its great horn is the first king. When it is broken, four kingdoms take its place, but not with its power.

scenes.title: A king of fierce countenance
scenes.text: Later a fierce king stands up. He destroys many, magnifies himself and even stands up against the Prince of princes. But he will be broken “without hand”, without any human power.

scenes.title: Daniel is left astonished
scenes.text: Gabriel says the vision of the evening and the morning is true, and it is for many days. Daniel is sick for some days. He goes back to work, still astonished, because no one understands the vision.

symbols.title: The ram with two horns
symbols.text: The kings of Media and Persia (verse 20). The two horns suit a kingdom made of two peoples. The higher horn came up last.

symbols.title: The goat and its horns
symbols.text: The king of Grecia, or Greece. The great horn is the first king. When it is broken, four kingdoms come out of the nation (verses 21–22).

symbols.title: Cleansing the sanctuary
symbols.text: Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, Israel’s sanctuary was cleansed. Hebrews says that sanctuary was a copy of the true one in heaven, where Jesus now serves as our High Priest.

connections.title: The bear and the leopard again
connections.text: The ram and goat match chapter 7’s bear, raised up on one side, and leopard with four heads. Chapter 8 names the kingdoms that chapter 7 leaves unnamed.

connections.title: The Prince of princes
connections.text: The little horn stands against the Prince of the host, the Prince of princes. Chapter 9 speaks of “Messiah the Prince” and chapter 12 of Michael, “the great prince”.

questions.question: Who are the ram and the goat?
questions.answer: The ram is the kings of Media and Persia. The goat is the king of Grecia, and its great horn is the first king.

questions.question: What happens at the end of the 2,300 days?
questions.answer: The sanctuary shall be cleansed.

questions.question: How does the fierce king finally fall?
questions.answer: He is broken without hand: no human power brings him down.

calculation.title: How long are the 2,300 days?
calculation.intro: Gabriel explains the ram and the goat, but not the time. Daniel says no one understood the vision. Chapter 9 picks up the question.

steps.title: 2,300 “evening-mornings”
steps.text: The sanctuary will be cleansed after 2,300 days. Verse 26 calls this the vision “of the evening and the morning”, the Hebrew way of saying full days.

steps.title: A long vision
steps.text: Gabriel says the vision is for the time of the end and for many days. It begins with Persia and reaches far beyond it.

steps.title: A day for a year
steps.text: As in chapter 7, a day in symbolic prophecy is read as a year.

steps.title: 457 BC to AD 1844
steps.text: This study follows Amazing Facts and begins the 2,300 years at the same point as the seventy weeks of chapter 9: the autumn of 457 BC. Counting 2,300 years from 457 BC, with no year zero, reaches the autumn of AD 1844, which Amazing Facts dates to October 22, 1844. Adventists understand this as the start of the judgment of Daniel 7 in the heavenly sanctuary.

interpretation.title: Where the little horn and the 2,300 days lead
interpretation.text: Daniel 8 names Media-Persia and Greece; it does not name the power that follows. Historicist readers see the little horn first as Rome, which rose after Greece and stood against Christ, and then as Rome in its papal form, which they believe drew attention away from Christ’s priestly work in heaven. Many other interpreters link this horn with the Greek king Antiochus IV. Historicists answer that this horn grows “exceeding great”, more than the powers before it, and that the vision reaches to the time of the end.

source: Adventist belief: Christ’s ministry in the heavenly sanctuary
Amazing Facts: Who Is the Antichrist?
reflection: Even when truth seems thrown to the ground, God has set a time to put things right. Where do you need to trust His timing?
prayer: Lord, You see what is hidden and You keep Your promises. Help me to trust Jesus, my High Priest. Amen.

heading: A humble prayer, and a promise of the Messiah.
time: Daniel 9 takes place in the first year of Darius the Mede (verse 1), after Babylon has fallen in chapter 5. Daniel is now old. Jeremiah’s seventy years of exile are almost over, and Daniel prays for Jerusalem. The 2,300 days of chapter 8 are still not understood, so Gabriel returns to explain.

scenes.title: Daniel reads Jeremiah
scenes.text: From the book of Jeremiah, Daniel understands that Jerusalem will lie in ruins for seventy years.

scenes.title: Daniel confesses
scenes.text: Daniel fasts and prays. He does not only blame others; he says “we have sinned”. He confesses that God is righteous and keeps His covenant, and that Israel did not listen to His prophets or obey His law.

scenes.title: Hear, forgive, act
scenes.text: Daniel asks God to turn His anger from Jerusalem and let His face shine on His ruined sanctuary. He asks, not because his people are good, but because of God’s great mercies.

scenes.title: Gabriel arrives
scenes.text: While Daniel is still praying, Gabriel comes at about the time of the evening offering. He tells Daniel he is greatly loved, and asks him to understand the matter and consider the vision.

scenes.title: Seventy weeks
scenes.text: Seventy weeks are set apart for Daniel’s people and city. In that time God will deal with sin, make reconciliation, bring in everlasting righteousness, seal up the vision and anoint the most Holy.

scenes.title: Messiah the Prince
scenes.text: From the command to restore and build Jerusalem to Messiah the Prince will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. After that, Messiah will be cut off, but not for himself. He confirms the covenant with many for one week, and in the middle of the week He causes sacrifice and offering to cease. The city and sanctuary will later be destroyed.

symbols.title: Seventy weeks
symbols.text: Seventy weeks are 490 days. With the day-for-a-year principle used in other prophecies, they are read as 490 years.

symbols.title: Messiah the Prince
symbols.text: “Messiah” means “Anointed One”. The New Testament word is “Christ”. Jesus was anointed with the Holy Spirit at His baptism.

symbols.title: Cut off, but not for himself
symbols.text: The Messiah dies, but not for His own wrongs. Isaiah says the Lord’s servant was “cut off out of the land of the living” for the sins of His people.

connections.title: Jeremiah’s seventy years
connections.text: Daniel’s prayer begins with God’s promise through Jeremiah that the exile in Babylon would last seventy years.

connections.title: “The time is fulfilled”
connections.text: After His baptism, Jesus began preaching with the words “The time is fulfilled”. Paul writes that God sent His Son “when the fulness of the time was come”.

connections.title: The sacrifices lose their purpose
connections.text: When Jesus died, the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom. Hebrews explains that His one sacrifice does what the repeated offerings only pointed to.

questions.question: Why does Daniel ask God to hear his prayer?
questions.answer: Not because of his people’s righteousness, but because of God’s great mercies.

questions.question: What starts the countdown to Messiah the Prince?
questions.answer: The going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem.

questions.question: What happens to the Messiah after the sixty-two weeks?
questions.answer: He is cut off, but not for himself.

calculation.title: Counting from the decree to the Messiah
calculation.intro: Daniel 9 gives the periods and their order, but not calendar dates. Each step below is marked as Bible statement, history or interpretation. There is no year zero, so one year is added when counting from BC into AD.

steps.title: 70 weeks
steps.text: Seventy weeks are 490 days. Read as prophetic days, they are 490 years.

steps.title: The starting point: 457 BC
steps.text: The countdown begins with the command to restore and build Jerusalem. In the seventh year of King Artaxerxes, in the autumn of 457 BC, a decree sent Ezra to Jerusalem with authority to set up its government under God’s law. It completed earlier decrees by Cyrus and Darius.

steps.title: 69 weeks to AD 27
steps.text: Seven weeks plus sixty-two weeks are 69 weeks, or 483 years. Counting 483 years from 457 BC reaches AD 27, which this study dates as the year of Jesus’ baptism, when He was anointed.

steps.title: The middle of the last week: AD 31
steps.text: In the middle of the final seven years, sacrifice and offering cease. This study reads this as Jesus’ death in AD 31, three and a half years after His baptism.

steps.title: The 70 weeks end: AD 34
steps.text: The 490 years end in AD 34. Around that time Stephen was killed, and the good news began to spread beyond the Jewish nation.

steps.title: The longer period: 2,300 years
steps.text: Gabriel came to explain “the vision” of chapter 8. So the 2,300 years start at the same point, 457 BC. The first 490 years end in AD 34; the remaining 1,810 years reach AD 1844, dated to October 22, 1844.

interpretation.title: Why this study applies the last week to Jesus
interpretation.text: This study follows the historicist reading, which applies all seventy weeks to the time of Christ without a gap. It reads “he” in verse 27 as the Messiah, who confirms the covenant. Many other Christians place the final week in the future and apply verse 27 to an antichrist. The dates above (457 BC, AD 27, 31 and 34) come from applying the text to history; Daniel 9 itself does not list them.

source: Biblical Research Institute: interpreting Daniel and Revelation
reflection: Daniel prayed “for thy great mercies”, not for his own goodness. How might you pray today in the same spirit?
prayer: O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive. Thank You for sending the Messiah at the right time. Amen.

heading: A heavenly messenger, and a conflict behind the scenes.
time: Daniel 10 begins the last vision of the book, which runs through chapters 10, 11 and 12. It is the third year of Cyrus king of Persia (verse 1), about 536 BC. Some Jews have returned to Jerusalem, but Daniel, now very old, is still in Persia, mourning and praying.

scenes.title: Three weeks of mourning
scenes.text: Daniel receives a message about a great conflict. He mourns and fasts from rich food for three full weeks.

scenes.title: A man clothed in linen
scenes.text: By the river Hiddekel (the Tigris), Daniel sees a man dressed in linen with a golden belt. His face is like lightning, his eyes like lamps of fire, and his voice like a crowd. Daniel’s strength leaves him, and he falls to the ground.

scenes.title: “Thou art greatly beloved”
scenes.text: A hand touches Daniel. He is told that his prayer was heard from the first day. The prince of Persia resisted the messenger for twenty-one days, but Michael came to help. Now he has come to explain what will happen in the latter days.

scenes.title: Strengthened
scenes.text: Daniel cannot speak or breathe. One like a man touches his lips and strengthens him. “Fear not: peace be unto thee, be strong.”

scenes.title: The scripture of truth
scenes.text: The messenger will return to fight with the prince of Persia, and the prince of Grecia will come. He will show Daniel what is written in the scripture of truth. Only Michael stands with him.

symbols.title: The man clothed in linen
symbols.text: John’s vision of the risen Jesus in Revelation 1 uses very similar words: a golden girdle, eyes like fire, feet like polished brass and a voice like many waters.

symbols.title: The prince of Persia
symbols.text: This prince resists a heavenly messenger for 21 days, so he is more than a human ruler. Many readers understand him as an evil spiritual power working behind the kingdom of Persia.

symbols.title: Michael
symbols.text: Michael is “one of the chief princes” and “your prince”, who stands for Daniel’s people. Jude calls him “Michael the archangel”, and Revelation shows Michael leading heaven’s army against the dragon.

connections.title: Prayer is heard at once
connections.text: God heard Daniel from the first day, even though the answer took three weeks. Jesus promised that the Father hears those who ask.

connections.title: An unseen conflict
connections.text: The book of Job and Paul’s letters also describe a spiritual struggle behind what happens on earth.

questions.question: When was Daniel’s prayer heard?
questions.answer: From the first day he set his heart to understand and humble himself.

questions.question: Who helped the messenger against the prince of Persia?
questions.answer: Michael, one of the chief princes.

questions.question: What did the messenger say when he strengthened Daniel?
questions.answer: “O man greatly beloved, fear not: peace be unto thee, be strong.”

interpretation.title: Who is Michael?
interpretation.text: The Bible calls Michael a prince, a chief prince and the archangel. Seventh-day Adventists and many Protestant interpreters through history have understood Michael as a name for Christ in His role as leader of heaven’s angels, not as a created angel. They point to the archangel’s voice at Christ’s return and to the “great prince” of Daniel 12:1. Other Christians understand Michael as a leading created angel. Both readings agree that Michael defends God’s people.

source: Biblical Research Institute: interpreting Daniel and Revelation

reflection: When an answer to prayer seems slow, what does Daniel 10 tell you about what may be happening unseen?
prayer: Lord, thank You for hearing me from the first day. Strengthen me and give me Your peace. Amen.

heading: Kings rise and fall; the time of the end draws near.
time: Daniel 11 is the messenger’s explanation, which continues from chapter 10. It begins in the days of Persia and follows the struggles of kings, “the king of the north” and “the king of the south”, all the way to the time of the end. It covers the same ground as chapters 2, 7 and 8, in much more detail.

scenes.title: Persia, then a mighty king
scenes.text: Three more kings will rule Persia, and a fourth will be very rich and stir up all against Greece. Then a mighty king will rule, but his kingdom will be broken and divided toward the four winds, not to his own descendants.

scenes.title: North against south
scenes.text: The king of the south and the king of the north make alliances and wars. Marriages, armies and treaties come and go. Some kings grow strong, others stumble and fall.

scenes.title: A vile person comes to power
scenes.text: A contemptible person takes the kingdom by flatteries. He works deceitfully and breaks “the prince of the covenant”. His heart is against the holy covenant.

scenes.title: The sanctuary polluted
scenes.text: Forces take away the daily and set up the abomination that makes desolate. Those who know their God will be strong. Many fall by the sword and flame, to refine and purify God’s people until the time of the end.

scenes.title: The king who exalts himself
scenes.text: A king will do as he pleases, exalt himself above every god, and speak marvellous things against the God of gods. He will prosper until the indignation is finished.

scenes.title: At the time of the end
scenes.text: At the time of the end, the king of the south pushes, and the king of the north sweeps through many countries and enters the glorious land. Troubling news makes him furious. He plants his tents between the seas and the glorious holy mountain, yet he will come to his end, and none will help him.

symbols.title: The mighty king and the four winds
symbols.text: The broken kingdom divided toward the four winds matches the goat’s great horn in chapter 8, which Gabriel named as the first king of Grecia.

symbols.title: The king of the north and the king of the south
symbols.text: North and south are described from Israel’s point of view. Early in the chapter they fit the Greek kingdoms that came after Alexander: the Seleucids to the north and the Ptolemies of Egypt to the south. Later in the chapter, the titles are applied to other powers.

symbols.title: The abomination that maketh desolate
symbols.text: Jesus pointed to this phrase from Daniel as something still future in His day, when He spoke of Jerusalem’s coming destruction.

connections.title: Pictures from earlier chapters
connections.text: The daily taken away and the sanctuary polluted repeat the words of chapter 8’s little horn. The king who speaks against the God of gods repeats chapter 7’s little horn.

connections.title: The man of sin
connections.text: Paul describes one who exalts himself above all that is called God, using language close to Daniel 11:36.

connections.title: Strong in God
connections.text: Even in this dark chapter, there is a promise for God’s people: those who know their God will be strong and do exploits.

questions.question: What happens to the mighty king’s kingdom?
questions.answer: It is broken and divided toward the four winds of heaven, not to his descendants.

questions.question: What does the chapter promise to people who know their God?
questions.answer: They will be strong and do exploits.

questions.question: How does the king of the north finally end?
questions.answer: He comes to his end, and none shall help him.

interpretation.title: A chapter readers explain in different ways
interpretation.text: Daniel 11 does not name its kings after Persia and Greece, so every reading of it is interpretation. Most interpreters agree that verses 5–20 describe the wars between the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms. Historicists then see the chapter move on to Rome, reading “the prince of the covenant” in verse 22 as the Messiah, and see verses 31–39 as the papal power of chapters 7 and 8. Adventist scholars do not all agree on verses 40–45, and this study does not give a detailed modern identification. Many others read verses 21–35 as Antiochus IV.

source: Biblical Research Institute: interpreting Daniel and Revelation

reflection: Kings rise and fall all through this chapter. What helps you stay strong when the news is full of conflict?
prayer: Lord, You know the end from the beginning. Help me to know You, and to be strong in You. Amen.

heading: Michael stands up, and God’s people are delivered.
time: Daniel 12 ends the vision that began in chapter 10, and it ends the book. It takes us to “that time”, the very end of the conflict in chapter 11. Daniel asks how long it will be, and he is told to go his way and rest, with a promise that he will rise again.

scenes.title: Michael stands up
scenes.text: At that time Michael, the great prince who stands for God’s people, stands up. There will be a time of trouble such as never was. But everyone found written in the book will be delivered.

scenes.title: Many wake from the dust
scenes.text: Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame. The wise will shine like the sky, and those who turn many to righteousness like the stars for ever.

scenes.title: Seal the book
scenes.text: Daniel is told to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end, when many will run to and fro and knowledge will increase.

scenes.title: How long?
scenes.text: Two figures stand by the river. One asks the man in linen how long until the end of these wonders. He swears by Him who lives for ever: it will be for a time, times and a half, and then all these things will be finished.

scenes.title: The wise will understand
scenes.text: Daniel hears but does not understand. He is told the words are sealed until the time of the end. Many will be purified, but the wicked will not understand. The wise will.

scenes.title: 1,290 days, 1,335 days, and rest
scenes.text: From the time the daily is taken away there will be 1,290 days. Blessed is the one who waits and comes to 1,335 days. Daniel is told to go his way: he will rest and stand in his lot at the end of the days.

symbols.title: The book
symbols.text: Those written in the book are delivered. Moses, Jesus and Revelation all speak of names written in God’s book of life.

symbols.title: Sleep in the dust
symbols.text: The Bible often calls death a sleep. Jesus said of Lazarus, “Our friend Lazarus sleepeth,” and Paul writes of the dead in Christ rising at His coming.

symbols.title: The sealed book
symbols.text: Parts of Daniel would not be fully understood until the time of the end (verses 4 and 9). Revelation 10 shows an angel with a little book open.

connections.title: The time of trouble
connections.text: Jesus spoke of great tribulation “such as was not since the beginning of the world”, using words close to Daniel 12:1.

connections.title: Shining like the stars
connections.text: Jesus said the righteous would shine like the sun in their Father’s kingdom.

connections.title: The resurrection
connections.text: Jesus said all who are in the graves will hear His voice and come out, some to life and some to judgment.

questions.question: Who will be delivered in the time of trouble?
questions.answer: Everyone found written in the book.

questions.question: What happens to those who sleep in the dust?
questions.answer: Many will awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

questions.question: What promise is Daniel given at the end of the book?
questions.answer: He will rest, and stand in his lot at the end of the days.

calculation.title: The 1,260, 1,290 and 1,335 days
calculation.intro: Daniel 12 gives three time periods. The Bible gives the numbers; the dates come from applying them to history, as Amazing Facts does.

steps.title: A time, times and a half
steps.text: The man in linen repeats the period of Daniel 7:25. As in chapter 7, it equals 1,260 prophetic days.

steps.title: 1,290 and 1,335 days
steps.text: Both periods are counted from the time the daily is taken away and the abomination that makes desolate is set up. A blessing is promised to the one who reaches the 1,335 days.

steps.title: From AD 508 to 1798 and 1843
steps.text: Following Amazing Facts’ charts, both periods begin in AD 508, when Clovis, king of the Franks, established the priesthood of the papal church. The charts link this with the “daily”: Christ’s heavenly ministry was displaced by an earthly priesthood. The 1,290 years end in 1798, when General Berthier ended papal supremacy. The 1,335 years end in 1843, when the Advent movement, which studied Daniel after 1798, was waiting for Christ’s coming. Verse 12’s blessing on “he that waiteth” is applied to them.

interpretation.title: Michael standing up
interpretation.text: Historicist readers understand Michael’s standing up as the moment Christ finishes His work as High Priest in heaven and takes up His kingdom. This is followed by the time of trouble and His return to deliver His people. Daniel 12 itself says Michael stands up, trouble follows, God’s people are delivered and many are raised. The order of events beyond that is drawn from other passages.

source: Adventist belief: Christ’s ministry in the heavenly sanctuary

reflection: Daniel’s book ends with the promise of rest and resurrection. How does that hope change the way you face the future?
prayer: Lord, write my name in Your book. Keep me faithful until the end, and raise me up with Daniel at the end of the days. Amen.
